This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance in finite samples, we conducted a comprehensive Monte Carlo experiment. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to real-world data sets, analyzing global stock market activity and Twitter activity during the 2013 Egyptian Revolution.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To meet this precision, we employed a careful calibration method that involves a LED, ensuring consistent imaging conditions and confirming the results with standard atmospheric theory.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in configurational averaging, outperforming other approaches by an order of magnitude in larger biomolecular simulations.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we argue that's not necessarily the best approach. Instead, we propose using visually normal users to assess the outputs of image description systems, which would serve as a viable alternative to existing description datasets. Such a process would involve presenting images to a group of users and asking them to provide a brief description, allowing researchers to test various system outputs against human judgments.

Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key advantage of this setting is its connection to a well-established mathematical framework known as the Knizhnik–Polyakov–Zamolodchikov (KPZ) fixed points. Building upon the research of Samouilov and Yuferev, this paper extends the solution space of the KPZ fixed point to include fixed-point solutions of the Euler–Arnold equation, thereby mapping out the full space of QFT complexity in this context.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points to resolve geometric inequalities, we obtain the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values.
Additionally, closed-form expressions for these values in a specific scenario are derived.
It is shown that the optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1] yields higher throughput in certain situations, but OFDM-based solutions provide stable and predictable performance.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since these processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can efficiently incorporate both theoretical predictions and experimental data. This paper presents a Python-based framework designed to facilitate the integration of diverse theoretical predictions and experimental data, featuring an initial implementation that outputs matched & evolved PDF candidate distributions, ready for fitting purposes.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. From this point forward, it's possible to derive the original nonlocal gravity theory in a form that can be verified experimentally, which is a deformed version of a source identity first presented by Dyson, Willey, Deser, and Jackiw. The modified, nonlocal gravity theory yields an identity that can be experimentally verified, similar to a nonlocal version of a vacuum identity in electrodynamics. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to the metric theory of gravity, for gravo-magnetic induction, and gravity-decay in vacuum.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC involving small systems studied
by the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Due to the growing significance
of QCD in small systems, particularly in situations with high multiplicity, not
all pertinent research can be covered within this report. It primarily examines
measurements focusing on collective behavior in small systems, discussing possible
interpretations where gluelballs may play a role and exploring observations that seem
to contradict hydrodynamical explanations. It also examines efforts to detect
quenched heavy quarks in small systems and discusses potential improvements in
seed gluon distribution models (LUXE) and the exploration of axial restoration in
small systems with an electric field.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study aims to investigate and analyze the outburst recurrence times of such neutron star binaries. To begin, we develop a framework based on the three main phases observed in the magnetized neutron star binary systems: an initial rapid recurrence phase, a period of increasing recurrence intervals, and a stage where the system may or may not enter a state of recurrence stability. To proceed, we analyze the distributions of recurrence times and a metric combining recurrence frequency and peak brightness of various neutron star binary systems. Building on this analysis, we propose that the source of confusion regarding the nature of these systems lies not in the potential for black hole misidentification, but in the lack of a clear understanding of the factors that determine the recurrence times of neutron star binaries.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number.

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, called HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous techniques and utilizes core coordination to improve performance degradation. While existing methods like TLM, PMOS, VMOS, and eye-diagram bias have limits in how much they slow down target processes without causing significant distortion, HyperDegrade can leverage core coordination to amplify timing differences. When applied to a Melcore audio video decoder, HyperDegrade was found to slow down specific attacks by up to 14.7x in comparison to other techniques, with a 50% reduction in resolution.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. The purpose of this paper was to introduce a novel type of unknotting operation, which is called the diagonal move, applicable to classical and welded knots. The study shows that the cross-over change, the delta-move, the sharp-move, the gamma-move, the n-gon move, the pass move, and the 4-move can be achieved by applying a sequence of diagonal moves. The study also delves into defining a distance measure that originates from the diagonal move, as well as examining its characteristics.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents must decide whether to cooperate. In this particular situation, an abandoned task is deemed uncooperative, whereas a shared task that requires cooperation is deemed cooperative. We analyze a game theoretic model of this situation in which the cooperative behavior of the agents reduces their individual rewards, ultimately leading to a evolutionarily stable strategy in which the agents prioritize their own interests. To overcome this limitation, we propose a simple communication protocol that allows the agents to infer the distribution of cooperation among the群体, providing them with additional information. We then extend the model to include this additional information, analyzing how the agents' strategies evolve based on their inferred knowledge of the群体.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the Cartesian Decomposition technique.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems with hundreds of antennas and high data rates face a new problem called non-overlapping visible regions when used in random access protocols. This issue arises due to a vast number of antennas and a user device having a limited number of radio chips, resulting in some data streams being inaccessible to specific groups of data recipients. Although this situation may appear disadvantageous, we find that it can be used to increase the capacity of multiple-user systems. In a proposed protocol, we exploit this phenomenon to reduce the traffic load on data streams in a multiple broadcast scenario with a large number of data recipients. As a result, data transmissions are targeted at smaller groups of recipients in various data sessions simultaneously, improving the overall system capacity. In a sample XL-MIMO system with 1024 antennas, we observe a 10% rise in capacity compared to conventional systems as the number of data sessions increases.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

This investigation seeks to examine the capabilities of Informed OCR (iOCR) in accurately capturing vote tabulation data, as the system is designed with an advanced spell-checking feature to correct common errors associated with traditional OCR technology, which the research reveals results in iOCR outperforming traditional OCR methods.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are reviewed that affect atmospheric circulation patterns, including methods to analyze the data obtained from the simulations. To further analyze the results, a series of experiments are conducted by gradually changing the temperature difference between the equator and the poles and the rotation rate of the planet. A new method is proposed to experiment with these factors, which involves varying the source of mid-latitude energy input to alter the temperature difference between the equator and the poles without suddenly changing the rotation rate. This approach helps avoid issues that may arise from abruptly changing the Coriolis effect on established atmospheric circulation patterns. By using this method, various circulation patterns observed in the experiments can be categorized into various types similar to those found in actual atmospheres on planets with atmospheres, including steady states, oscillating patterns, and chaotic variations. Three distinct energy-driven circulation patterns in the model are identified that resemble three major mid-latitude atmospheric circulation patterns observed in actual atmospheres on terrestrial planets, including the Ferrel cell, baroclinic waves, and polar vortex, as well as three corresponding instabilities leading to these patterns, as well as three corresponding large-scale atmospheric circulation patterns on terrestrial planets that can be considered equivalent to the three major modes of convection observed in the model.

This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. It also proves the connection to the traditional complex representation, in addition to obtaining a modified complex representation following the standard Hankel path.

Tackling the challenges posed in Section 2, we have derived explicit expressions for the time derivatives of the density and current operators in their quadratic forms. These expressions incorporate the effects of quantum potential and quantum pressure within stochastic hydrodynamic form, enabling a leap to probabilistic hydrodynamics. This method utilizes a Weiner process to mitigate the imaginary component of the wavefunction's evolution, facilitating a transition to classical/ stochastic hydrodynamics. This evolution utilizes a Weyl-Moyal star product to diminish the higher-order terms in the quantum potential and pressure, promoting a transition to classical/ stochastic hydrodynamics. As a result, we have obtained an operator-valued stochastic hydrodynamic equation that incorporates the effects of interacting Bose gases (BBGKY hierarchy). This equation utilizes the density and current operators in quadratic forms, enabling a transition to a phase-space stochastic hydrodynamic description. This picture utilizes coupled Weyl operators to mitigate the effects of interacting Bose gases (Bogoliubov approximation), yielding a dynamical equation with the probabilistic hydrodynamic description. This equation utilizes Weyl operators in a Fock space, which can be interpreted as a local quantum field, enabling a description as a local classical/ stochastic field. This local field drives the Fokker-Planck evolution of a density operator in phase space. As a byproduct, we have gained insight into the description of Bose gases in terms of vortices (Xiong-Rehberg). This description utilizes Fock space

Deep Neural Networks with vast parameters have faced challenges in real-time deployment, prompting the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge distillation. Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research leveraging Teacher-Student architectures has successfully combined multiple knowledge-learning objectives with efficient, lightweight student networks. This distinct survey delves into the specifics of Teacher-Student architectures with multiple knowledge learning objectives and systematically explores knowledge construction and optimization processes, as well as analyzing various Teacher-Student architectures and learning schemes that produce robust and representative knowledge. Moreover, the paper summarizes and highlights the practical applications of Teacher-Student architectures across various purposes, such as classification, recognition, and generation, before exploring promising research directions, particularly on the design of Teacher-Student architectures, the quality of knowledge, and the theoretical studies of regression-based learning. With its in-depth analysis, this survey is poised to provide invaluable insights for industry, academia, and policymakers on the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in multiple knowledge learning objectives.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to the special linear Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ and $n$ of its copies. As a result, the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be presented in a new way using the special Racah algebra, offering a novel perspective on the special variant. As a concluding step, the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be derived from the defining relations of the special Racah algebra.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. We resolve this issue by developing an efficient exact paired-permutation test method. Our algorithm can accurately determine the significance of results in a paired NLP system evaluation, allowing for a precise calculation of the test statistic's p-value. This capability is particularly useful in developing combined evaluators that leverage multiple metrics and models.

An experimental observation of the triangular flow coefficient ($v_3$) in heavy ion collisions indicates that quark-gluon fluid exhibits an exceptionally high degree of collective motion and possesses extremely low viscosity. To verify if an ideal hydrodynamic model can accurately predict $v_3}$ in both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions, we have conducted a more in-depth analysis. By varying collision energies and participating particle numbers, we generated multiple data points for both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at a specific particle ratio of 0.2, then utilized the JAM multiphase transport model to predict these data points. To obtain a broader sample of Cu+Cu collision data, we generated 14 sets of Cu+Cu collision data at various Npart values using a scaling method based on the assumption that $v_n$ is proportional to $1/Npart} for specific centralities in Au+Au collisions.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter predicts the density of unobserved targets, with their distribution approximated as Gaussian for initially detected targets. A new implementation that incorporates a tree-structured angular sector quantization pattern is also presented. An application demonstrating the use of a control law to minimize estimation error covariance, while considering control information limits, is introduced as well

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy in most situations. The results indicate an improved chance of scoring when teams possess the ball in pivotal situations, leading to a more significant point gain as a team's performance improves. We also observed that professional players' situations differ from lower-league players in terms of intensity. As part of the study, we created a three-dimensional graph to visualize the situation-specific values and an action-value table to display the results.

The surge in telework due to the COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the need for instrument control software that supports remote operation. This is particularly pertinent to particle measurement systems like Laser Doppler Velocimetry (LDV), which often require complex optical setup. In this study, we demonstrate the effective remote operation of a LDV system using a single probe point to perform two-dimensional velocity measurements. A customized controller software was developed to automatically adjust the system and conduct measurements at multiple points. The software's capability to reliably map and record velocity profiles along a two-dimensional plane is highlighted, paving the way for creating 3D velocity profile maps with a three-point LDV system.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral long-lived particles relies on either finding decay products at unusual locations or missing energy. The choice between these methods depends on the particle's properties, as well as those of the detector used. To better understand the effectiveness of these methods, we are examining how they complement each other, with a focus on the Belle II experiment and axion-like particles produced through the decay of certain mesons. A new detection approach for these particles, which involve a two-body decay process where a meson transforms into another particle and then a form of missing energy, has been proposed. This strategy, using data from Belle II equivalent to $50$ times its current amount, should allow the experiment to discover particles of a very low mass that leave little trace, with certain characteristics that include a minimum production probability and a minimum time that the particle remains active. This detection method is anticipated to significantly improve the discovery potential of Belle II for these types of particles by as much as two orders of magnitude. The most efficient way of detecting these particles, which could weigh a few hundred million times less than an electron, would involve searching for decay products at unusual locations and analyzing energy data from various experiments involving the collision of high-speed particles, which include those carried out in experiments involving the decay of certain mesons in the Belle II experiment and in experiments involving the collision of protons in the LHCb experiment.

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present a refined ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend the grammatical and
semantics components of words, differing from issues seen with static
embeddings. We propose multiple possible avenues for resolving these issues
in the future.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic effects, and the AGN model itself, a non-linear fitting procedure reveals the characteristics of heavy AGNs. This fitting indicates that in heavy AGNs with high optical luminosity and low radio luminosity, most have high black hole spins Greater than 0.9, making them ideal for the search of ultra-light bosons through the mechanism of gravitational energy extraction via superradiance. This search focuses on the Ramsay-Sermillas process, investigating the formation of boson clouds around rotating black holes, which cause spin degradation. Considering the minimum heavy AGN spin inferred and the assumption of reaching an equilibrium state through the Ramsay-Sermillas process, upper limits on the growth rate of boson instability are determined. This leads to upper limits on the ultra-light boson coupling constant $\epsilon$, connecting it to the boson mass through the growth rate of superradiance. The resulting constraints on the coupling constant and mass of bosons expand upon previous constraints derived from the observation of rapid X-ray timing variability around black holes, and are

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. The lattice QMC method produced identical results to the analytic solution and the path integral/MCMC method, demonstrating the reliability of these approaches in computing expectation values for non-stationary states. The path integral MCMC method, in particular, provided a valuable tool for complex simulation situations where analytical solutions were not readily available.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the models' performance, and finally, the study proposes a straightforward correction method to address the bias. The results reveal that the bias persists across different inversion codes but can be significantly mitigated by incorporating ff into the analysis. A simple post-processing step demonstrates a more effective resolution of the problem, especially when combined withff. The research underscores the necessity of accurately reconstructing the neutral component, ff, to accurately resolve the vector magnetic field.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given that numerous loss functions are available, including cross entropy, Kullback-Leibler divergence, and squared error. Despite its importance, the subject has seen very little empirical research, leaving us with theoretical explanations that lack specificity. Our study fills this gap by conducting a systematic investigation into the role of loss function in deep learning, exploring its impact based on the context, the type of neural network architecture employed, and the task being undertaken. Through experimentation, we discovered that various data sets exhibit distinct characteristics, revealing that cross entropy is typically the most effective loss function, with Kullback-Leibling and squared error often underperforming. The results also highlight the importance of data normalization when using squared error. Furthermore, the study reveals that different neural network architectures exhibit varying performance when using different loss functions, with UShape showing the most significant differences in some data sets. To expand our understanding, we also examined the behavior of ensemble models when using combination loss functions, revealing unique results. Finally, we explored the underlying causes for the observed outcomes, analyzing the mathematical properties of cross entropy, Kullback-Leibling, and squared error, as well as the characteristics of the data sets being classified.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an extensive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning inferences, organized as a tree of over 40000 synthetic scenarios. This atlas of knowledge fills a crucial gap in the domain of machine learning research, offering a robust resource for developing and evaluating more advanced models. Each situation described in ATOMIC consists of a starting point and a set of possible next steps, with annotated information outlining the most likely outcome. This format enables a variety of reasoning tasks, including the prediction of subsequent events, classification of relationships between cause and effect, and the drawing of inferences based on observed situations. Such capabilities are essential for navigating dynamic environments and interacting effectively with others, and can be integrated into both static NLP tasks and dynamic domains such as gaming and virtual assistants.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on single viewpoint prediction, our goal is to develop a technique that generates videos from unseen viewpoints, offering a significant leap in visualized performance for virtual reality applications. To achieve this goal, we've created a model that combines two representations - a geometric module based on GAN architecture and an appearance module utilizing an LSTM network - to facilitate the generation of videos from unseen perspectives. GANs are utilized to handle novel view synthesis in a geometric manner, ensuring a distortion-free output, while LSTM networks are employed to GANs' output to refine the appearance, preserving temporal dependencies. To validate the efficacy of our proposed model, we've created a new dataset consisting of multiple views recorded from six dynamic scenes and conducted extensive experiments on three established datasets.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found their average conditions to be significantly non-equilibrium. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation mechanism to be influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. It also prevents the use of these specific lines for temperature measurement and suggests utilizing heavily populated low-J molecular lines, such as CO(010) and CO(101), which are in LTE and averaged temperature to be in the range of 18-20K. This temperature is in agreement with dust temperature measurements. We also found the (C{\sc i})/(CO) brightness temperature ratio to be ineffective in determining excitation temperature due to its correlation with density and not temperature, and we found it to be a star formation indicator when normalized to the CO lines. Based on a 3-level system in steady-state, we derived a new star formation indicator, the S(2000)/S(1000) ratio, which is independent of temperature and density and is correlated with the (C{\sc i})/(CO) ratio.

Our research establishes that in ASEP, a system with binary particles and a first-order speed variation involving five distinct values, each ASEP lattice point corresponds to a specific ASEP speed lattice point where information propagates. Additionally, we provide a ASEP speed process that is ergodic, consisting of five equivalent representations, derived from an irreducible Markov process that is L0-preserving and that is implemented on ASEP speed configuration space.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, that lack practical significance.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events in real-time. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events present a cold start problem, as there is a lack of similar historical examples for existing models to draw upon, makes the problem even more complex. To address this challenge, a novel end-to-learning system has been proposed that enables the model to detect false information on unexpected events without the need for similar labeled historical examples. This achieved outcome demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed system in capturing an underlying concept of fact verification in a fact-versus-oxide task in a combined approach in a meta learning framework in a neural process setting in an emergent outcome in an emerging machine learning space in a vast dataset of similar events in an extensive range of similar situations in a wide variety of similar contexts in a broad spectrum of similar scenarios in a multitude of similar instances in a plethora of similar cases in a host of similar examples in a battery of similar tests in a array of similar analyses in a series of similar studies in a string of similar observations in a sequence of similar events in a set of similar situations in a group of similar contexts in a cluster of similar scenarios in a collection of similar instances

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge graph like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach to identify the join irreducible submodules. Leveraging the association between submodules and the module's composition factors, we can reconstruct the lattice of submodules of a given module from knowledge of the lattices of submodules of its factors and their intersecting submodules. Additionally, we examine the structure of this reconstructing process and its resulting lattice.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, we identify subsets whose definability is equivalent to subsets definable by logic with a quantifier, extending results beyond the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is fit with CLN and BGL form factor parametrisations to derive key parameters for both models.

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. Otherwise, the trend towards more complex behavior with increased traction velocity is confirmed through a burstein-like sudden increase in noise intensity at the ultimate speed. Otherwise, the impact of adhesion mechanisms on noise dynamics is highlighted by conducting the experiment under air, oil, and vacuum conditions.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems.

Point-cloud neural networks often suffer from shaky performance when it comes to certain token permutation rules. To tackle this issue, we create a smoothing technique called "Transformation-Specific Smoothing (TPC)" to improve point-cloud neural network accuracy. We start by focusing on permutation rules that maintain a consistent x-coordinate order and expand their scope to other 2D smoothing strategies without losing their effectiveness. Our experimental results show that our TP method yields better outcomes compared to existing techniques, boosting Model Accuracy by as much as 70.4% in K-Nearest Neighbor classification, 41.3% in DeepGCN network models, and 372.6% in DeepSets network models.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of Serre's conjecture related to GL_2 through Kummer theory, thereby bypassing the reliance on p-adic Hodge theory. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices, including sparse and dense matrices, and is applicable in various fields such as statistics, econometrics, and machine learning.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. Contexts are assumed to be generated randomly and a new approach is presented. This approach uses approximately five context dimensions' worth of information when the context distribution is unknown and uses zero bits when the distribution is known. This approach offers nearly the same regret bound that would be achieved if contexts were fully known. This indicates that the proposed approach is informationally efficient and nearly optimal. This indication is particularly notable when context dimensions are substantial and is validated through theoretical analysis. This analysis provides a lower bound that aligns with the proposed approach's bound when the context distribution is known. A further enhancement is also mentioned.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases. Its effectiveness in triggering instability is influenced by the distribution of dust within these systems. This research examines the VSI in a refined model that takes into account dust evolution processes, analyzing both linear stability and growth rates of instability. Without considering dust evolution processes, a system is found to be susceptible to VSI, resulting in rapid growth rates in certain regions. When taking into account the coupling between gas and dust, analysis shows that settlement of heavier particles at the midplane suppresses VSI growth. Further investigation reveals that a more massive system leads to a greater susceptibility to VSI. By considering a model that includes dust evolution processes, VSI is found to be limited due to dust settlement, resulting in a reduction of instability growth rates by an order of magnitude. To enhance VSI effectiveness in盘 systems with evolved dust distribution, suggestions are made to decrease the surface of new particle formation or increase the initial mass of the system.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service (MLaaS) have created innovative opportunities but have also introduced novel threats, prompting the development of various attacks, particularly in deep learning contexts. In this context, backdoor attacks have proven to be highly effective but typically require an attacker to have prior knowledge of an innocuous update rule or an embedding poisoner tool. However, this requirement can be a significant limitation in many scenarios. To address this context, this research has created an update rule that integrates a hidden trigger into a DL model's output features following a GAN-like structure's learning process, specifically in its final GAN stage. This integrated backdoor manifests its malicious behavior only after the model has been deployed, making it undetectable during the learning process. This research has utilized a GAN architecture, a GAN variant, a GAN-like structure, a GAN-like backdoor, a GAN-like attack, a GAN-likeGAP, a GAN-like objective function, a GAN-like optimizer, a GAN-like post-processing step, a GAN-like pre-processing step, a GAN-like layer, a GAN-like activation function, a GAN-like loss function, a GAN-like metric, a GAN-like dataset, a GAN-like training technique, a GAN-like evaluation method, a GAN-like attack method, a GAN-like GAN, a GAN-like GAN variant, a GAN-like GAN structure,

In the context of a parameter serverless model, a deep learning random walk algorithm has been a significant area of research. A gradient random walk method was proposed to address a logistic regression problem with non-independent and identical distributed data, aiming to achieve consensus on models and facilitate data learning. A more generalized multi-step random walk learning algorithm was also introduced to solve this problem, demonstrating its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and random walk planning. A logistic regression example with data-biased scenarios was used to validate the randomness of the proposed algorithms, highlighting their ability to overcome data bias and achieve learning objectives.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses simple consistency regularization, ensuring that segmented images of mixed or interpolated input annotations remain unchanged. This approach aligns with an implicit assumption made in many existing semi-supervised learning models. To test the technique, three different input interpolation methods were evaluated on three well-known medical image segmentation datasets. The results show that this simple regularization method produces segments closely matching those of complex regularisation techniques. Building on this finding, a more advanced method can be developed by incorporating additional factors into its approach.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment, in which a spin-1/2 particle becomes entangled with a spatial degree of freedom following a magnetic field gradient, to illustrate this instantaneous non-locality of the wave function collapse. Notably, we depict how this non-locality can be utilized to establish single-particle entanglement between the particle's spin and spatial degrees of freedom. Consequently, single-particle entanglement is shown to embody a novel feature that is unique to quantum mechanics, by giving rise to truly non-local effects, including single-particle steering, that cannot be explained by local hidden variable models.

This paper presents a comprehensive review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning (BEFL) for Internet of Vehicles applications, beginning with an in-depth examination of Blockchain technology in safety-critical Internet of Vehicles applications, and followed by an overview of privacy-preserving techniques in image and video data. The core portion of this review outlines the principles of BEFL frameworks, highlighting the synergistic benefits of combining Blockchain and Federated Learning for Internet of Vehicles applications. The article concludes by outlining potential research directions in this emerging field, pecking order of critical issues, and a summary of the article's key findings. The proposed BEFL literature review is believed to be a valuable resource for both industry practitioners and academia in developing next-generation Internet of Vehicles applications.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests.

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of a subgroup of the symmetric group for a field of sufficiently large characteristic. Moreover, for any given subgroup G of the symmetric group, there exists a specific characteristic that allows the (m-folded) iterated composite polynomial's iterate to exhibit this particular Galois group.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in a limitless, uniform environment. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through a mass concentration argument, is improved upon by analyzing the concentration of energy through a variational framework associated with a ground state solution.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the successful convergence of multiple simulation models under examination. In an attempt to address these challenges, we have developed a workflow that integrates a variety of automated and manual techniques to ensure the reliable estimation of Bayes factors. This bayesfactor-R package facilitates model comparison using Bayes factors in R, while the proposed framework outlined in this paper ensures accurate behavior of simulation models for effective hypothesis assessment.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which discloses intricate relationships between indicators and discourse instances.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, modified in the $r$-symmetrized format, meets the requirements for a 2-cocycle. Additionally, we have obtained specific formulae for its associated star product and twisted coproduct. Furthermore, we have established that our generalized version is equivalent to a Drinfel'd twist proposed by Eshaghi Gordi et al. (arXiv:1206.6293).
